state.misconception_label: Adds when calculating volume instead of multiplying

turn_history.speaker: student
turn_history.text: I have: The volume of this cuboid is \( 30 \mathrm{~cm}^{3} \) What length should replace the star? ![A cuboid, depth 2cm and height 3cm. The width is labelled with a star.](). I got \( 25 \mathrm{~cm} \) because I'm not sure I worked it out the right way.

turn_history.speaker: teacher
turn_history.text: Imagine you have a box of chocolates where each row has 2 chocolates and there are 3 rows stacked on top of each other. If you add the number of chocolates in each row, you wouldn't get the total number of chocolates in the box, right? It's the same idea with calculating the volume of a cuboid - you need to multiply the dimensions together to find the total volume. So, to find the correct length to replace the star, you'll need to multiply the depth and height of the cuboid with the width. Can you try that now?

turn_history.speaker: student
turn_history.text: Okay, I think I get what you're saying about multiplying instead of adding. So, if I multiply the depth (2 cm) and height (3 cm), I get \( 6 \mathrm{~cm}^{2} \). But then how do I use that to find the width? Do I just divide the total volume by that \( 6 \mathrm{~cm}^{2} \)?

turn_history.speaker: teacher
turn_history.text: Imagine you have a rectangular swimming pool with a length of 2 meters and a width of 3 meters. If you want to find the total area of the pool, you wouldn't divide the total area by the length or width, right? Instead, you would multiply the length and width together to find the total area. Similarly, to find the width of the cuboid, you need to divide the total volume by the product of the depth and height. Can you try that now?

turn_history.speaker: student
turn_history.text: Okay, I think I understand a bit better now. So if I have the volume \( 30 \mathrm{~cm}^{3} \) and I already found that \( 6 \mathrm{~cm}^{2} \) from multiplying the depth and height, I can divide \( 30 \mathrm{~cm}^{3} \) by \( 6 \mathrm{~cm}^{2} \) to find the width. But what does that give me? Is it just the width in cm?

score.justification_pass1: The teacher effectively addresses the adding-versus-multiplying misconception with clear analogies, and the student progresses from adding (getting 25) to correctly applying division, though Turn 3's swimming pool analogy confusingly discusses area when the student had already grasped the multiplication concept and just needed confirmation about division.
score.justification_pass2: The teacher consistently grounds abstract volume concepts in concrete, relatable real-world analogies (box of chocolates, swimming pool) that connect directly to the mathematical operations being taught.
